content_voiceover: This graph is a classic board favorite because it explains the biphasic and paradoxical early risks of starting warfarin. Each clotting factor and natural anticoagulant declines at a rate determined by its own half-life, since warfarin only blocks new synthesis of active factor, it doesn't clear what's already circulating. Factor seven has the shortest half-life at four to six hours, so it drops fastest, followed closely by protein C at about eight hours. Protein S, factor nine, factor ten, and prothrombin, factor two, decline much more slowly, with prothrombin's half-life stretching to forty-two to seventy-two hours. The clinical danger here is that protein C, a natural anticoagulant, falls almost as fast as factor seven in the first day or two, while the procoagulant factors two, nine, and ten are still nearly at baseline. That transient imbalance, more anticoagulant depletion than procoagulant depletion, creates a brief hypercoagulable window, which is the mechanistic basis for warfarin-induced skin necrosis and why we bridge with heparin when starting warfarin in patients with active clotting, especially those with underlying protein C deficiency.
keypoints: Factor VII (4-6h) and protein C (8h) fall fastest after starting warfarin
Prothrombin (factor II) falls slowest, half-life 42-72 hours
Early transient drop in protein C before procoagulant factors clear creates a hypercoagulable window
This explains warfarin-induced skin necrosis and the need for heparin bridging
keypoint_voiceover: Factor seven and protein C fall fastest, while prothrombin lingers the longest. That mismatch creates an early hypercoagulable window, which is why warfarin can cause skin necrosis and why we bridge with heparin at initiation.
